chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said:

I was sitting with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and with him was only his son Ja'far. He said, 'O Zurarah, Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) and Uthman disputed during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). Uthman said: 'For every wealth of gold or silver that is circulated, worked with, and traded in, zakat is due when a year passes over it.' Abu Dharr said: 'As for what is traded in, circulated, and worked with, there is no zakat in it; rather, zakat is due in it only if it is rikaz (buried treasure) or a stored treasure (kanz). When a year passes over it, zakat is due in it.' They disputed this matter before the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and he said, 'The verdict is as Abu Dharr said.'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to his father, 'What do you want by bringing forth something like this, so that people will stop giving to their poor and needy?' His father said to him, 'To you from me; I cannot avoid it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between zakat on trade goods and stored treasure according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a juristic dispute between Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and Uthman ibn Affan regarding the definition of taxable trade assets, with the Prophet affirming Abu Dharr’s view that zakat applies specifically to wealth held for investment or stored as treasure. Imam al-Baqir’s subsequent remark underscores the practical implication of this ruling: clarifying the scope of zakatable goods prevents the general public from withholding charity due to uncertainty. This incident is pivotal in Shia fiqh for distinguishing between commercial capital and personal consumption goods.
